THE CHAPTERS
By Albert C.
Washington's Birthday, 1884, saw
the nineteenth jewel added to our
fraternal crown. On that memorable
day at the installation of the Eta
my father observed that after more
than hak a
century "the badge, the
name, the methods, and the objects
(of Psi Upsilon) remain the same."
Today, with our Fraternity nearly
one hundred and eight years old,
the observations of the author of the
Epitome hold fast. Our cherished
diamond badge, our
mystic symbols,
our democratic Constitution and or
ganization, and our fraternal devo
tion-remain a
priceless heritage.
Mellowed ui tradition, they have
stood the test of time. So soundly
did our Fathers build, so firm the
foundation stones laid by our
great
pioneers, that Psi Upsilon has had
the power and the vitality to face
OF PSI UPSILON
Jacobs, Phi '21
a world of change, to adapt itself
to the vicissitudes of life. From ad
versity, from depression, from the
ravages of war our Chapters have
emerged triumphant, stronger and
more independent.
Since our fraternal fires were
lighted in 1833 on the altar of the
Theta, twenty-eight other "dear old
shrines"�from New York to the
Golden Gate, from Maine to Van
couver�have been kindled. At the
end of a decade the calcium light
beamed from ten historic colleges.
During the next forty years but
eight more shrines were installed. In
our second half century ten were
hghted, to be followed at the dawn
of our second hundred years with
the kindling of stiU another. With
such loving care and vision did our
brothers of an earlier day select the
akars of our Fraternity that from
aU but two gleams the beacon hght
of venerable Psi Upsilon, a record un
paralleled in fraternity annals. The
altar fires at Cambridge and New
Haven have, to the great sorrow of
every member of Psi Upsilon, be
come extinguished, not because of
any weakness in the Alpha and the
Beta, but because internal conditions
peculiar to Harvard and Yale, mihtating against fraternities, made it
difficult for those famous Chapters
of our Fraternity to "keep our
temple
walls still bright."
The Story of the Chapters of Psi

Annals of
Upsilon is a
story of 1882 years of
Chapter life. The embryonic period
adds many years to this total. The
Beta Beta was
thirty-eight years old,
the Nu twenty, and the Epsilon Phi
twenty-four, when for them the ivied
gates were unbarred. The first ef
forts to erect shrines in Williams and
Wisconsin were made sixty-three and
forty-six years respectively before
they were successful. The Iota, Phi,
Pi and Mu all battled long and ardu
ously for a
Chapter of Psi Upsilon.
The Theta, Delta and Sigma have
celebrated their centennials. Within
the next two years the Gamma, Zeta,
Lambda, Kappa, Psi and Xi will have
run a course of one hundred years
of glorious brotherhood.
This is the history of 1882 years
of Chapter life, 1882 years of growth
of independent and autonomous
groups, groups that have never, thank
goodness, been subject to strong cen
tralized control. Our Chapters, pri
vileged over the years to fight their
own battles and to meet their own
peculiar problems, have in their strug
gle to survive grown stronger, have
everywhere developed an interest in
and a
loyalty for Alma Mater. They
stand today after 1882 years of life
as the finest examples of democracy
�in their annual Conventions they
legislate on
problems pertaining to
the Fraternity at large�in the Coun
cil they have an executive but not
a
governing body. It is our
pride that
the undegraduates guide Psi Upsilon;
that in our Halls they gain experi
ence invaluable in later days; that
our
Fraternity stands as an
integral
part of Alma Mater. How fitting fiiat
Psi Upsilon, tracing its heritage to
Phi Beta Kappa, which was born in
the year of our
independence, should
pSi UPSILON
cherish as it has done the sacred
traditions of democracy!
Because our Chapters are autono
mous, self-governing bodies, they
have fortunately not adhered to one
pattern. They have built, as their
policies have dictated, a Fraternity
whose strength lies in the different
types composing it, all being united
before the altar of Psi Upsilon.
To tell the story of the Chapters
of Psi Upsilon is a
privilege and an
obligation. It is a
responsibility to
our seven hallowed Founders, to the
many pioneers who built our
temple
walls, to our
great historians, Wil
liam Taylor, Theta '38, WiUard Fiske,
Psi '51, and Albert P. Jacobs, Phi
'73, who have in words that can
never be matched painted the maj
esty and the glory of our fraternal
Order. It is an
obligation to the
22,000 persons who have been privi
leged to wear the diamond badge
over their hearts. To narrate 1882
years of Chapter life and many more
of embryonic existence, years in
which 22,000 human souls have
carved the destinies of Psi Upsilon, is
a monumental undertaking. Few
have been privileged to wend their
way over the path which in the
course of eleven decades has led from
the Mohawk Valley to the Canadian
outpost on the Pacffic;
To sing again the good old songs.
The mystic bond stiU bless;
to foUow in the footsteps of Taylor,
Fiske, and my father. It is with meek
humility that I deign to retrace the
history as told by these masters, and
to embark upon the enormity of my
task. My father 'wrote of 554 years
of Chapter life in nineteen Chapters,

But in 1915, six years after the

Epitome should include

In 1920 the Convention adopted a

mond and that the Psi Upsilon Club

Six years later the Council out
lined plans for Chapter histories so
that at the time of the great Centen
nial a new
Epitome might be issued
which would contain a
complete his
tory of each Chapter. From then on
Convention after Convention have
urged the completion of Chapter
histories. In 1927 alumni representa
tives were called together in New
York for the support of The Diamond,
Chapter histories and the archives.
At long last efforts which began
ninety-six years ago are about to
bear fruit. The Chapters of Psi Upsi
lon could not have been written

Psi Upsilon, a
pioneer in the fra

The valuable experience gained in

Our Chapters all have some form

strong
alumni association. They have played

Psi Upsilon was born on Novem
ber 24, 1833, in a
quaint Dutch set
tlement on the banks of the Mohawk.
Union College, then but thirty-eight
years old and situated in Schenec
tady, at that time a
village of four
thousand inhabitants, has justly been
called "The Mother of American Col
lege Fraternities." By 1833 old Union
had already become a leader in the
academic Ike of the country. Cer
tainly outside of New England it was
the foremost educational institution
in the United States. To its halls
Union attracted a remarkable body
of students from far and near. Per
haps because of youth and the lack
of high bound tradition, Union pre
ceded the more venerable institutions
of New England in departing from
the narrow classical training.
The early days of old Union are
well described by one of America's
leading historians and the present
President of the CoUege, Dr. Dixon
Ryan Fox:
Most of the time from 1825 to 1850
Union College was the largest in the United
States. Several different years Yale got
ahead of it, but Harvard and Princeton
were behind and . . . Columbia was much
behind. There is no
question but that in
1833 Union was the leader. This was not
due so much to its location or its fine
buildings as to its faculty and particularly
its President, Dr. Ehphalet Nott. Dr. Nott
was a remarkable man.

An eloquent preacher, an out
standing inventor, a leader in hu

of the country's foremost educators.
As President from 1804 to 1866, for

His main power was teaching and in

students from other institutions. . . . Union
was
thought of as a sort of senior college

The records for the year 1833

lege in that year had transferred

were
sixty-six seniors, eighty-three

dents. Dr. Nott's liberal attitude in

It has been said that Dr. Nott was

Six of the leading fraternities were

., being desirous of a more close and
